HuMoTAR: Physics-Aware Agentic Retargeting for Humanoid–Object Interaction

Narayanan Palghat Parameswaran1 Jay Karhade1 Haoyang He2 Neehar Peri3 Jay Patrikar2 Dong-Ki Kim2 Shayegan Omidshafiei2 Sebastian Scherer1,2 Deva Ramanan1
1Carnegie Mellon University 2FieldAI 3California Institute of Technology

Key Takeaways

  • Existing human-to-humanoid retargeting methods optimize kinematic alignment, which does not guarantee that a motion’s semantic intent is preserved under physical execution. We posit that frontier agentic models can capture both the semantic intent and physical requirements of a motion for generalizable retargeting.
  • Closed loop simulation feedback allows LLM agents to iteratively refine the robot motion and control. We evaluate humanoid retargeting through object-tracking errors and semantic scoring (LLM-as-Judge) to measure motion fidelity and completion of the intended task.
  • We study the compute-time tradeoff between deploying an agentic swarm and longer single-agent iterative refinement. Under a fixed time budget, a four-agent swarm outperforms a single Codex agent by 20% in LLM-scored semantic success rate, but a compute-matched Codex agent surpasses the swarm by 7.5%, at 4x the time.
  • Experience from related tasks, stored as summaries of tested strategies and their outcomes, improves success on new tasks. On a novel humanoid-object task, prior furniture-moving experience reduces mean object-tracking error from 23.35 cm to 7.77 cm and turns a semantic FAIL into a PASS at equal compute and time.

1. Rethinking humanoid retargeting

Consider the human demonstrations above, in which a person carries a chair, moves a clothes stand and tilts a bin with one foot. For a humanoid to perform these tasks, each demonstration must first be adapted to its body, since a humanoid differs from a human in proportions, joint limits and actuation. Current human-to-humanoid retargeting methods largely formulate it as a kinematic problem, in which the human’s motion is fitted to the robot while relevant contacts with the environment are preserved. HOI-Retarget, for example, optimizes the robot’s motion to match the demonstration’s body poses and object-relative contacts. This raises the question of what a humanoid should preserve from a demonstration.

We argue that retargeting should preserve the intended task rather than the precise movements a human uses to perform it. Take, for example, a person who carries and places a chair with one hand. The goal is to carry the chair to a target location and place it there, not to exactly reproduce the one-handed grasp motion. A humanoid may use both hands if its morphology and physical limits allow it, since the task is unchanged even though the grasp and posture differ from the demonstration. In our experiments, we scale the demonstrated object trajectory to the robot’s size and use it as the target motion. The robot’s contact strategy, posture and controller are free to change.

A kinematically feasible reference is not necessarily dynamically feasible. SPIDER addresses this by posing retargeting as a constrained optimization over the robot’s motor commands. It samples many candidate command sequences in a physics simulator and keeps the ones whose simulated motion stays closest to the reference. However, errors in the input motion reference can lead SPIDER to the wrong contact strategy. Its open-loop execution is also sensitive to the robot’s starting pose.

We posit that frontier agentic models provide useful priors for making these changes. We explore the use of LLM agents to write, test and iteratively revise motion and control code through closed-loop simulation feedback. We refer to this general approach to agentic semantic retargeting as HuMoTAR.

Carry and place a chair

Lift, carry and place a clothes stand

The above examples illustrate the gap between kinematic retargeting and physical execution. We execute the kinematic references provided by HOI-Retarget using SPIDER in physics simulation and compare them with HuMoTAR’s references. SPIDER fails to complete either task, while HuMoTAR achieves successful execution in physics simulation in both cases.

2. Comparing agentic workflows for humanoid retargeting

We compare HuMoTAR with SPIDER’s execution of the kinematic references generated by HOI-Retarget. Using GPT-6 Astra, we study iterative refinement with simulation feedback in three agentic configurations: a single Codex agent, an independent agentic swarm and a collaborative agentic swarm. We also evaluate Astra one-shot without tool calls or iterative refinement.

We compare these configurations under a fixed time budget and an equal compute budget measured in agent-hours to study the compute–time tradeoff between agentic swarms and longer single-agent iterative refinement.

  • Astra one-shot generates motion and control code in one response, without tool calls or further revisions.
  • Codex tests and revises its solution in a persistent coding session.
  • Independent agentic swarm runs four Codex agents that develop their solutions independently.
  • Collaborative agentic swarm runs four Codex agents that can communicate directly with one another to share findings, request help and critique strategies.

For each task, the inputs to HuMoTAR are the human demonstration in SMPL format, an initial kinematic reference from HOI-Retarget, the task scene and the target object trajectory. The object trajectory is scaled for the robot and specifies the desired object motion. The agents write Python code to generate and refine a reference motion for the whole body and hands, which is the output of the framework.

The motion references and control code are executed in MuJoCo with SONIC as the whole-body controller. After each simulation, the agent inspects images of the execution, object-tracking errors and contact measurements. The available feedback is described in the appendix.

3. Retargeting results and analysis

Evaluation metrics

Results cover 20 HUMOTO and 20 OMOMO tasks. We report object-tracking errors and semantic success for each comparison.

Object tracking. We compare the object’s pose in the simulated execution with the human-reference object trajectory scaled for G1. The target trajectory stays fixed, and the object’s size is unchanged. We align the two paths by progress through translation and rotation rather than elapsed time, so the robot can move at a different speed or pause.

  • Mean ADD (cm): at each aligned pair of object poses, we measure the distances between corresponding points on the object. The average over points and the trajectory captures both position and orientation error.
  • Position error (cm): the average distance between the simulated and target object origins.
  • Orientation error (°): the average angle between the simulated and target object orientations.

All three errors are averaged equally across tasks. Lower is better.

Semantic success. Astra compares the human demonstration with the robot execution and judges whether the intended object interaction is completed. Exact timing, posture and grasp need not match. We report the percentage of tasks judged PASS, after a separate review for obvious initial hand–object penetration. Incomplete executions count as unsuccessful. Higher is better. The evaluation protocol includes the judge prompt and review criteria.

3.3 The effect of inter-agent communication

Per-task tracking errors and semantic judgments · 40 tasks

The collaborative swarm succeeds on ten tasks that the independent swarm fails, and regresses on two. Its mean ADD is lower on 24 of 40 tasks. The logs contain direct messages, shared controller files and independent tests of peer proposals, including proposals that are rejected after testing.

This establishes that communication affects the refinement process, rather than merely accompanying it. It does not isolate how much of the result comes from reuse, critique or different sampled strategies. We report the exchanges and both directions of outcome change in the communication analysis.

3.5 The compute–time tradeoff

Final results only. Mean ADD uses the 39 tasks with valid executions in all plotted conditions; semantic success uses all 40.

The collaborative swarm reaches 67.5% semantic success in 30 minutes. Two-hour Codex reaches 75% in 120 minutes. Both are allocated two agent-hours: four agents for half an hour, or one agent for two hours. The observed tradeoff is a shorter completion budget versus a higher final success rate. Agent-hours describe the allocation, not identical token consumption or simulation work. Budget definitions and comparison limits.

4. Inside the refinement process

4.1 How does the agent refine an interaction in simulation?

We begin with a human demonstration and an initial G1 motion from HOI-Retarget. The scaled object trajectory defines the interaction goal, while the robot's motion and controller remain open to refinement. Figure 5 shows how Astra turns this starting reference into a program that can be executed, inspected and revised in simulation.

Astra writes executable Python code. The code can construct wrist trajectories, solve inverse kinematics for arm and waist joints, adjust finger targets, and change the duration of individual motion phases. Across the recorded runs, agents also implement joint-impedance control, object-pose feedback and contact-dependent transitions; some try constrained inverse dynamics to compute joint torques. These strategies are implemented in the generated program, together with any revised reference trajectories and initialization.

Physical execution requires whole-body control to support the robot and hand control to manipulate the object. We use SONIC as a frozen whole-body policy, tracking a motion reference at 50 Hz. Its 29 body joints include the arms and wrists, but not the Dex3 fingers. To control the interaction, Astra writes a custom hand and arm controller in Python. This controller commands the fingers and, when needed, replaces SONIC’s arm commands with targets, gains and feedforward torques suited to the task.

The agent can also revise the motion reference supplied to SONIC so that whole-body control follows the intended arm motion. During each rollout, SONIC and the custom hand and arm controller produce the joint commands. Astra inspects the resulting execution and revises the code or reference before the next trial.

MuJoCo executes the combined joint commands and records the resulting robot and object motion. Astra can inspect rendered views, tracking errors, contact locations and forces, joint limits and collision clearances. It uses this feedback to revise the next candidate, then tests the complete interaction again. The retained result includes the executed reference motion and the controller needed to replay it. The examples in Figure 5 show the kinds of changes made within this loop.

4.3 Tracking error during refinement

A kinematic reference specifies the intended motion, but execution can produce large errors when contact fails or the robot cannot support the load. Figure 7 follows the performance of the iterative refinement process over a 30-minute budget. Each step reflects a new best execution as the agent revises the motion or controller. The dark curve averages across all tasks; the lighter curves show HUMOTO and OMOMO separately. The larger drops indicate substantial improvements, followed by smaller corrections as refinement progresses.

Mean ADD selects the best execution at each point; position and orientation report that same execution. The curves begin when all tasks have a scored execution; the unrefined kinematic replay was not recorded consistently enough to mark a shared starting value.

4.4 How much refinement can a shorter budget retain?

Early stopping limits the time spent on iterative refinement while retaining the best reference motion output obtained so far. Here, the stopping condition is elapsed refinement time: at a chosen cutoff, we retain the reference motion output and its controller from the refinement stage with the lowest measured mean ADD for each task. We evaluate this condition retrospectively using the recorded executions and token usage from the full 30-minute runs.

Figure 8 marks the average time each task takes to reach 90%, 95% and 99% of its recorded ADD reduction. The 95% milestone averages 22.3 minutes, which motivates a 22.3-minute early-stopping cutoff. Stopping every task at that time retains 88.4% of the improvement on average, because individual tasks reach their milestones at different times.

5. Does experience matter?

Yes, related experience helps in the shelf-righting example, but the benefit depends on what transfers to the new task. Reports from other furniture interactions help G1 complete the lift, reducing mean ADD from 23.35 to 7.77 cm compared with continuing without experience. Both continuations start from the same checkpoint and receive the same refinement time.

Comparing refinement with and without experience

We investigate whether experience from related interactions helps a robot retarget a new task. Here, G1 must raise a shelf from lying on its side to standing upright. The experience consists of reports from four other furniture tasks, including carrying a table and lifting a chair. These reports summarize the strategies tested and their outcomes.

We first run four agents for 15 minutes, two with optional access to the provided retargeting tools, and select the best valid shelf motion. From this checkpoint, we run two separate 15-minute continuations: one receives the reports, and the other continues without them. Both use the same model, tools and starting solution, with 30 minutes of total refinement. This comparison measures the benefit of the supplied experience under an equal refinement budget.

Righting a shelf with related experience

6. Discussion

Limits of the metrics

We posit that retargeting should be evaluated by the successful transfer of an interaction’s semantic intent. In this study, object tracking provides a measurable objective for preserving the intended object motion. It is possible, however, for executions with similar tracking errors to differ in how fully they accomplish the task. User studies could complement these measurements by assessing whether the intended interaction is preserved. LLM-based judges could also supply semantic feedback during refinement and evaluation. We encourage the community to explore these directions and assess their agreement with human judgments.

RL fine-tuning

Humanoid references can serve as training data for downstream whole-body policies. Our results demonstrate the promise of agentic refinement using off-the-shelf models and low-level controllers, without training a new policy for each interaction. Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning could build on these references to improve robustness to disturbances and variation in the task scene. Downstream policy training and deployment remain to be evaluated. We hope this work encourages the community to investigate agentic methods as a source of reference motions for learning interactive humanoid systems.

Failure cases in dynamic retargeting

Our approach still struggles with thin objects and difficult contact geometries. In the plate example, the robot lifts the plate but does not complete the human’s swirling motion. Across the recorded attempts, agents revise finger placement and try two-handed support, yet the grasp remains unreliable during rotation. We observe that contact strategies must account for the robot’s hand morphology. The Dex3 fingers must establish opposing contacts around a thin, sloped rim, which appears to contribute to the difficulty of this task. Motion and controller refinement do not yet resolve this limitation.

How does HuMoTAR compare on kinematic retargeting?

We compare GMR, HOI-Retarget and HuMoTAR on the same task set.

We follow HOI-Retarget’s evaluation protocol (Appendix A): body pose deviation, link velocity direction error, contact-point gap and relative hand-orientation change measure how well the robot preserves the human motion and object-relative contacts. We also report body jerk as a smoothness measure, the mean magnitude of the third time derivative of the palm, ankle, head and pelvis positions, estimated by finite differences. Lower values indicate smoother motion.

Can a text description replace a motion reference?

We give a single Codex agent a detailed task description, the scene and an initial robot–object state, without a human motion reference or target object trajectory. The agent has 30 minutes to refine an execution that follows the description, using SONIC for the legs and waist and custom arm and hand control. These five examples show the supplied commands and the resulting simulated motions.

Lift and inspect a basket

Text command

A basket rests on the floor in front of the person. Bend toward it and reach down with the right hand to take its handle. Lift the basket clear of the floor while straightening the body. Bring it in front of the torso, then use the other hand to help steady and turn it for inspection. Tilt and rotate the basket so its opening and different sides can be examined, rather than simply holding it motionless. Keep it under control throughout the lift and the changes in orientation. Finish standing with the basket held in front of the body; the demonstrated sequence ends while it is still being held.

Lift, lower and lift a side table

Text command

A small wooden side table with a raised curved rail stands on the floor in front of the person. Bend down, grasp the raised rail and lift the table off the floor as the body straightens. Keep the tabletop approximately level and the legs directed downward. Lower it back onto its legs in front of the body, then pause with the table supported on the floor. Bend toward it again and repeat the lifting action. Make the separate pickup, lowering, supported pause and renewed pickup recognizable, rather than replacing them with a single static hold or dragging the table along the floor. Remain near the table and keep each movement controlled.

Walk and turn while carrying a side table

Text command

Hold the small wooden side table with both hands in front of the torso, keeping its legs clear of the floor. Walk while carrying it along a curved path that turns the body through several facing directions, then comes back toward the starting area. The table travels with the person and turns with the body; its legs remain generally downward and the tabletop remains approximately level, with natural tilting during the turns. Keep both hands supporting the table while stepping and changing direction. Finish the walking sequence still holding the table in front of the body. The interaction should show sustained transport and turning, not stationary lifting or sliding on the floor.

Lift, move and set down a clothes stand

Text command

Stand beside a tall freestanding clothes stand with a circular base and branches near the top. Reach to its vertical pole around waist height with one hand. Lift its base clear of the floor, then take a few steps to move the stand to a nearby position while keeping the pole mostly upright. Move the body together with the stand rather than reaching from a fixed stance. Lower the circular base onto the floor, allow the stand to settle upright, and release the pole. Finish beside the independently standing object with the hand withdrawn. The lift, short transport and deliberate placement should be clearly visible.

Rock a wooden chair and return it upright

Text command

Face a wooden chair and bend toward it, placing both hands around the sides of the seat or nearby frame. Tilt and rock the chair so its seat and back lean and one pair of legs rises while the other pair remains near the floor. Guide the chair back toward an upright orientation and bring all four legs down under control. Keep the hands engaged while the chair changes orientation, and adjust the body with the movement. Finish with the chair upright and supported on its legs. This is a controlled rocking and righting interaction, not carrying the chair away or allowing it to fall.
How is semantic success evaluated?

The same Astra judging prompt compares the complete human demonstration and robot execution. A PASS means the main object interaction is substantially achieved. A FAIL means an essential action is missing or the object is lost before completion. An UNCERTAIN judgment is not counted as a pass. The prompt permits differences in robot posture, grasp and timing, as well as minor wobble or imperfect placement.

A separate opening-contact review checks for obvious initial hand–object penetration. Normal contact, small overlaps and ambiguous occlusion are not disqualifying. Suspected substantial intersections are reviewed with additional views; a collision-proxy measurement alone does not establish penetration. This review can change a PASS to a FAIL without modifying the original judge response. It is not a collision audit of the entire motion.

Success rates use all 40 assigned tasks. The two-hour Codex condition has one incomplete execution, counted as unsuccessful. Tracking comparisons with this condition use the same 39 valid tasks for both methods. The other final tracking comparisons use all 40 tasks.

Original judging prompt 
You receive two videos:
- Reference: the original human–object interaction.
- Candidate: the robot execution.

Does the candidate achieve the overall object interaction shown in
the reference?

Judge generously. Focus on what happens to the object across the
complete motion. Exact trajectory, timing, robot posture and grasp
need not match. Minor wobble and imperfect placement are acceptable.

PASS if the main interaction is substantially achieved.
FAIL if an essential part is missing or the object is lost before
the interaction is completed.

Check object rotation across multiple frames. Do not mistake an
intentional set-down for a drop. Do not require release or a stationary
ending unless the reference clearly makes it part of the interaction.

If the view does not provide enough evidence, return UNCERTAIN
instead of guessing.

Return:
- Verdict: PASS / FAIL / UNCERTAIN
- Reason: one or two sentences citing visible moments in the candidate.
What simulation feedback can the agents inspect?

After a rollout, agents can inspect rendered views and numerical measurements from the recorded execution:

  • Robot and object motion: images of the execution and recorded poses and joint states.
  • Object tracking: mean ADD, position error and orientation error relative to the target object trajectory.
  • Contact: contact locations, normals and forces, including which robot and object surfaces touch.
  • Geometry and motion checks: contact gaps, penetration, joint-limit margins and differences between reference and executed motion.

Agents can inspect these outputs with code and request further views or measurements. The observations they use depend on the trial; each iteration does not necessarily inspect every measurement.

Which tools and control interfaces can the agents use?

Agents can write their own analysis and control code. Two ensemble agents also receive a supplied retargeting-tools file, which they may use, modify or replace. These helpers expose the following measurements and interfaces; they do not prescribe a grasp or a refinement sequence.

Table A2. Interfaces available during refinement.

Tool or interface What it provides
Contact inspection Contact locations, normals and forces from a saved execution, with close-up views.
Geometry checks Contact gaps, surface alignment, penetration and joint-limit margins for a proposed pose.
Motion diagnostics Link-position and orientation errors, and reference, command and execution joint traces.
Object-path evaluation Mean ADD, position and orientation errors against the fixed target trajectory.
Whole-body control A frozen tracking policy driven by a motion reference.
Custom joint control Targets, gains and feedforward torques for the agent’s manipulation controller.

Do the independent workers produce different solutions?

All 30 tasks with four full 30-minute worker records have distinct final motion hashes among their valid workers. Their mean best-worker ADD is 20.12 cm, compared with 30.74 cm for the within-task median worker. This measures variation in executed outputs and the effect of selecting the lowest-error output. It does not measure diversity of strategies or prove that workers avoid redundant experiments.

The remaining ten historical HUMOTO results use four 15-minute workers followed by a 15-minute continuation of the selected worker without experience. Their initial worker spread is reported separately below. They contribute to the published final results, but not to the 30-task worker-spread means above. The historical independent and later collaborative runs are therefore not a controlled communication-only ablation.

Two independent-swarm PASS verdicts were disqualified by the separate initial-penetration review. The adjusted success count is 19/40, equal to 30-minute Codex. Seven tasks change from FAIL to PASS and seven from PASS to FAIL.

What did the collaborative workers actually exchange?

The audit covers all 160 workers across all 40 tasks. It counts successful, completed communication calls, with duplicate event IDs checked across resumed sessions: 1,797 broadcasts through publish_findings, 3,238 direct messages through message_peer and 2,127 calls to read_peer_updates. These are tool calls, not estimates from prose summaries.

159 workers ran at least one successful shell command referencing a shared peer_files path. This includes reading and copying files as well as testing them. It is not a count of adopted controllers. The command audit also finds direct simulator invocations with a peer controller path, but a command alone does not establish that its rollout completed or improved the result.

The examples below show the content of the exchanges. They illustrate mechanisms present in the logs; they are not used to estimate their frequency or explain every outcome change.

sub11 monitor 044 · worker 00

Retrieved capped15 and running independent replay. I will sweep root feedback strengths with your capped15 (80/25cap25 baseline,120/40cap40,210/70cap50, desiredrootvelocityFF option). You handle cap size sweep. Adaptivephase decoupledbody failed/ejected at5s; not adopting.

The final task outcomes are listed in the paired comparison, including the ten gains and two regressions. Fewer repeated trials, better strategy diversity and a causal effect of critique have not been established by these counts. Those claims would require classifying executed revisions and repeating the comparison under the same protocol.

What improves within the same two-hour run?

For each cutoff, we retrospectively select the lowest-ADD recorded execution that had finished by that time. It must have completed its reference and passed the recorded initial-object-pose and zero-velocity checks. The framework scores every trial against the same complete target trajectory. All three displayed errors come from the execution selected by ADD. Position and orientation errors can therefore increase even when ADD decreases.

Active time is reconstructed from the original call and each resume's stated remaining budget. Documented interruption gaps are excluded. Independently generated final verification replays are excluded from intermediate selection. This is a retrospective analysis of saved outputs, not a claim that an agent had computed every comparison score at that instant.

35 tasks have an eligible output by 30 minutes. On that fixed paired set, mean ADD falls from 30.17 to 10.65 cm and 33 tasks improve. Comparing the selected 30- and 120-minute manifests, reference-file hashes change on 31 tasks and initial-state hashes on 26. A changed hash establishes an artifact change, not its purpose or a semantic improvement. The other five tasks remain visible below without an invented early value.

Semantic comparisons reuse the existing Astra judgments for the separate 30-minute and 120-minute Codex experiments, with their existing opening-contact reviews. These are final-output judgments, not judgments of intermediate outputs within the two-hour runs. No new replays or judgments are part of this analysis.

The final, separate-run semantic comparison has six Codex-only successes and three swarm-only successes. The judges describe missing rotation, transport or placement in the six gains, and incomplete release or loss of the object in the three regressions. This describes the final videos. It does not establish when those actions first became successful within the longer runs.

What is matched in the compute–time comparison?

The collaborative swarm receives four 30-minute worker budgets, totalling two agent-hours. The longer Codex condition receives one 120-minute budget, also totalling two agent-hours. Allocated agent-hours do not equate token counts, simulation counts, accelerator usage or native delegated-agent work.

The final semantic comparison includes all 40 tasks and counts the incomplete two-hour submission as unsuccessful. Tracking uses the same 39 valid final executions for both methods: 13.00 cm ADD for the collaborative swarm and 12.63 cm for two-hour Codex. The within-run table above uses different, retrospective selections and must not be substituted for these final submitted results.

Each condition has one recorded run per task. Differences between conditions combine workflow, budget and sampling effects. The within-run analysis tests whether later recorded outputs improve over earlier ones, but repeated runs would be needed to establish how reliably a workflow produces that improvement.
